passages.text: Pressure-stabilized superconductive yttrium hydrides

The search for high-temperature superconductors has been focused on compounds containing a large fraction of hydrogen, such as SiH<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, CaH<sub>6</sub> and KH<sub>6</sub>. <sentence_start/>Through a systematic investigation of yttrium hydrides at different hydrogen contents using an structure prediction method based on the particle swarm optimization algorithm, we have predicted two new yttrium hydrides (YH<sub>4</sub> andYH<sub>6</sub>), which are stable above 110 GPa. <sentence_start/>Three types of hydrogen species with increased H contents were found, monatomic H in YH<sub>3</sub>, monatomic H+molecular “H<sub>2</sub>” in YH<sub>4</sub> and hexagonal “H<sub>6</sub>” unit in YH<sub>6</sub>. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, H atoms in YH<sub>6</sub> form sodalite-like cage sublattice with centered Y atom. <sentence_start/>Electron-phonon calculations revealed the superconductive potential of YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> with estimated transition temperatures (<italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub>) of 84-95 K and 251-264 K at 120 GPa, respectively. <sentence_start/>These values are higher than the predicted maximal <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> of 40 K in YH<sub>3</sub>.

The study of hydrogen-rich compounds at hig pressure is mostly motivated by their potential high-tempeature superconducivities at high pressures. <sentence_start/>In 2004, Ashcroft<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b1" pmid="15169525" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.92.187002" count="1">1</citation> suggested that hydrogen-rich compounds can become metallic and superconducting at lower pressures than hydrogen, preumably because of “chemical compression”. <sentence_start/>Since then, theoretical studies have revealed a large number of superconducting hydrides (SiH<sub>4</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b2" pmid="18339933" doi="10.1126/science.1153282" count="1">2</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b3" pmid="18764567" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.077002" count="1">3</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b4" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.087005" pmid="19257780" count="1">4</citation>, SnH<sub>4</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b5" pmid="17501079" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.117004" count="1">5</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b6" doi="10.1073/pnas.0908342107" pmcid="PMC2824346" pmid="20080576" count="1">6</citation>, GeH<sub>4</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b7" pmid="18851245" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.107002" count="1">7</citation>, ScH<sub>3</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b8" doi="10.1073/pnas.0914462107" pmcid="PMC2840305" pmid="20133755" count="1">8</citation>, YH<sub>3</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b9" pmid="19792676" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.077002" count="1">9</citation>, GaH<sub>3</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b10" count="1">10</citation>, H<sub>2</sub>S<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b11" pmid="24811660" doi="10.1063/1.4874158" count="1">11</citation> <italic toggle="yes">et al.</italic>) at high pressures with predicted <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> ranging from 17 to 86 K. Remarkably, our previously prediction of high <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> (80 K at 160 GPa) in H<sub>2</sub>S<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b11" pmid="24811660" doi="10.1063/1.4874158" count="1">11</citation> has been proven recently from experiments<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b12" count="1">12</citation>. <sentence_start/>Recently, a new type of hydrogen solvated molecular complex SiH<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has been synthesized<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b13" doi="10.1073/pnas.0907729106" pmcid="PMC2736422" pmid="19706419" count="1">13</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b14" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.065701" pmid="19792585" count="1">14</citation> and was predicted to have a <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> of ~100 K at 250 GPa<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b15" doi="10.1073/pnas.1007354107" pmcid="PMC2936615" pmid="20798059" count="1">15</citation>, which is much higher than the 17 K observed in SiH<sub>4</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b2" pmid="18339933" doi="10.1126/science.1153282" count="1">2</citation>.The experimental and theoretical studies have led to further investigations on hydrides with large hydrogen fraction that may provide a pathway to better superconductors. <sentence_start/>Using first-principle structure predictions, Zurek <italic toggle="yes">et al.</italic><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b16" doi="10.1073/pnas.0908262106" pmcid="PMC2764941" pmid="19805046" count="1">16</citation> first predicted three new lithium hydrides (LiH<sub>2</sub>, LiH<sub>6</sub> and LiH<sub>8</sub>) above 130 GPa, which are stabilized by charge transfer from Li to H. <sentence_start/>Subsequent studies have revealed a number of hydrides with large hydrogen fractions at high pressures, such as Na-H<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b17" pmid="21770539" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.106.237002" count="1">17</citation>, K-H<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b18" count="1">18</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b19" count="1">19</citation>, Rb-H<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b20" pmid="22392860" doi="10.1002/chem.201103205" count="1">20</citation>, Cs-H<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b21" pmid="22897718" doi="10.1021/ic301045v" count="1">21</citation>, Ca-H<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation>, GeH<sub>4</sub>-H<sub>2</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b23" pmid="21033810" doi="10.1063/1.3505299" count="1">23</citation> and H<sub>2</sub>S-H<sub>2</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b24" pmid="22243091" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.255503" count="1">24</citation>. <sentence_start/>Remarkably, some hydrides were predicted to possess high <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub>, e.g., ~82 K in LiH<sub>6</sub> (300 GPa)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b25" doi="10.1107/S2053229613028337" pmid="24508954" count="1">25</citation>, ~70 K in KH<sub>6</sub> (166 GPa)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b18" count="1">18</citation> and strikingly ~235 K in CaH<sub>6</sub> (150 GPa)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation>.

Among the different hydrides, yttrium hydrides (YH<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>) are of special interest because each Y atom has three valence electrons and, in principle, could be shared with three H atoms. <sentence_start/>Experimentally, that during the continuous absorption of H atoms, a reversible transition of YH<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic> between the reflecting YH<sub>2</sub> and optically transparent YH<sub>3</sub> was observed. <sentence_start/>This interesting phenomenon offers a great potential for practical application as a “switchable mirror”. <sentence_start/>Raman<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b26" count="1">26</citation> and infrared<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b27" count="1">27</citation> studies found that the semiconducting YH<sub>3</sub> transforms to a metallic fcc structure above 10 GPa. <sentence_start/>Singnificantly, fcc-YH<sub>3</sub> was predicted to be a superconductor with <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> of 40 K at 17.7 GPa, the lowest reported pressure for hydrides to date<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b9" pmid="19792676" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.077002" count="1">9</citation>. <sentence_start/>The prediction, however, has not been confirmed by experiment.

At high pressure, it is expected that the valence electronic state of Y atom will change and therefore provides a possibility of bonding with more H atoms. <sentence_start/>Here, we focus on the formation of Y hydrides with larger H concentration at high pressures of YH<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8). <sentence_start/>Two new thermodynamically stable hydrides with stoichiometries of YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> were found above 110 GPa. <sentence_start/>Electron-phonon calculations show both YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> are superconductive with relatively high <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub>.
Results

The enthalpies of the candidate structures of YH<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic> found in structure predictions relative to the products of dissociation into Y + solid H<sub>2</sub> and YH<sub>3</sub> + solid H<sub>2</sub> at selected pressures are summarized in Fig. 1 (a,b), respectively. <sentence_start/>Fig. 1 (a) shows all the stoichiometries considered here possess negative formation enthalpies with respect to Y + solid H<sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>Among those, YH<sub>3</sub> has the lowest energy. <sentence_start/>Two thermodynamically stable polymorphs, YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub>, are to be thermodynamically more stable than the decomposition into YH<sub>3</sub> + sold H<sub>2</sub> were found at 140 and 160 GPa (Fig. 1b). <sentence_start/>Although YH<sub>2</sub>, YH<sub>5</sub> and YH<sub>8</sub> have negative formation enthalpies with respect to Y + solid H<sub>2</sub>, they are expected to decompose at all pressure. <sentence_start/>For example, YH<sub>2</sub> decomposes into YH<sub>3</sub> + Y since the enthalpy is above the tie-line connecting YH<sub>3</sub> and Y. <sentence_start/>Similarly, YH<sub>5</sub> and YH<sub>8</sub> decompose into YH<sub>4</sub> + YH<sub>6</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>, respectively (Fig. 1b). <sentence_start/>Therefore,YH<sub>2</sub>, YH<sub>5</sub> and YH<sub>8</sub> are excluded in the discussions hereafter.

So far, YH<sub>3</sub> is the only experimentally known yttrium hydrides at high pressure. <sentence_start/>The structure search readily reproduced the observed fcc structure<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b26" count="1">26</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b27" count="1">27</citation> at 100 and 150 GPa. <sentence_start/>As can be seen from Fig. 2 (a), there exist only one type of Y atom occupying the fcc site and two nonequivalent, H1 and H2, atoms at the octahedral and tetrahedral sites. <sentence_start/>The H-H separation is of 1.9 Å at 120 GPa, clearly indicates no interaction between the H atoms (Fig. 2d). <sentence_start/>Therefore, the H atoms in fcc-YH<sub>3</sub> are monoatomic. <sentence_start/>fcc-YH<sub>3</sub> was previously predicted to be stable in a large pressure region of 20 GPa<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b28" count="1">28</citation> to 197 GPa<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b29" count="1">29</citation> and undergo a superconductor - metal - superconductor transition under pressure<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b9" pmid="19792676" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.077002" count="1">9</citation>.

Figure 1 (c,d) show the formation enthalpies of YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> with respect to YH<sub>3</sub> + solid H<sub>2</sub> as functions of pressure. <sentence_start/>The formation enthalpy of YH<sub>4</sub> becomes negative relative to YH<sub>3</sub> + solid H<sub>2</sub> near 128 GPa (Fig. 1c). <sentence_start/>It is important to include the quantum nuclear zero-point energies (ZPE) when considering the energetics of systems containing light atoms. <sentence_start/>We therefore calculated the ZPEs of YH<sub>4</sub>, YH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> phases within the quasi-harmonic approximation. <sentence_start/>When ZPE corrections are included, the predicted pressure for the onset of stability of YH<sub>4</sub> is lowered to 112 GPa (inset in Fig. 1c). <sentence_start/>The stable YH<sub>4</sub> has a tetragonal structure (space group <italic toggle="yes">I</italic>4/<italic toggle="yes">mmm</italic>, denoted tI10 hereafter, Fig. 2b) with two formula units per unit cell. <sentence_start/>We found that the tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> has the same structure type with tI10-CaH<sub>4</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation>. <sentence_start/>The tI10 structure at 120 GPa consists of body-centered arranged Y atoms and two nonequivalent H1 and H2 atoms with H1-H2 and H2-H2 distances of 1.58 and 1.33 Å, respectively. <sentence_start/>Valence electrons localization was found between the two neighbouring H2 atoms while absent between H1 and H2 atoms (Fig. 2e). <sentence_start/>This indicates the presence of both molecular “H<sub>2</sub>” and monoatomic H in tI10-YH<sub>4</sub>.

YH<sub>6</sub> becomes thermodynamically more stable than YH<sub>3</sub> + solid H<sub>2</sub> above 122 GPa (Fig. 1d). <sentence_start/>The onset pressure of the stability of YH<sub>6</sub> is reduced to 110 GPa when considering the ZPE effect (inset in Fig. 1d). <sentence_start/>In the thermodynamically stable pressure region, YH<sub>6</sub> adopts a cubic structure with space group <italic toggle="yes">Im</italic>-3<italic toggle="yes">m</italic> (2 f.u./unit cell, denoted cI14 hereafter, Fig. 2c). <sentence_start/>The “H<sub>6</sub>” hexagons are forming a corner-shared sodalite-like cage with a Y atom at the center, the same sodalite structure found in CaH<sub>6</sub> above 150 GPa<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation>. <sentence_start/>In this case, the H-H distance of 1.31 Å at 120 GP is longer than in CaH<sub>6</sub>. <sentence_start/>Despite the longer distance, covalent interaction between H atoms is clearly visible from the localized valence electrons between the H atoms (Fig. 2f).
Discussion

We found three types of H species in YH<sub>n</sub> compounds, monatomic H in YH<sub>3</sub>, monatomic H+molecular “H<sub>2</sub>” in YH<sub>4</sub> and hexagonal “H<sub>6</sub>” in YH<sub>6</sub>. <sentence_start/>Since molecular H<sub>2</sub> has a filled covalent <italic toggle="yes">σ</italic> bond, the additional electrons donated from Y will occupy the antibonding <italic toggle="yes">σ</italic>* bond, resulting in a stretched or even dissociated H-H bond. <sentence_start/>For example, the formation of YH<sub>3</sub> can be described by the reaction 2Y + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2YH<sub>3</sub>. <sentence_start/>Assuming all 6 valence electrons (3 from each Y atom) were transferred to the H<sub>2</sub>, then, each H<sub>2</sub> would accommodate two additional electrons into the σ* orbital and, thus, breaking the H<sub>2</sub> molecule into monatomic H. <sentence_start/>Integration of the electron density shows that each H1 (H2) atom in fcc-YH<sub>3</sub> have accommodated an additional 0.54 (0.47) electrons. <sentence_start/>A similar description can be used for the formation of YH<sub>4</sub>. <sentence_start/>In this the reaction is Y + 2H<sub>2 </sub>→ YH<sub>4</sub>. <sentence_start/>There are three electrons available to two H<sub>2</sub> molecules. <sentence_start/>Therefore, one H<sub>2</sub> bond is completely broken into two monoatomic H and the remaining electron occupied the <italic toggle="yes">σ</italic>* one the second H<sub>2</sub>, thereby weakening the bond and resulted in a longer H-H distance of 1.33 Å. <sentence_start/>The additional charge of the monatomic H1 in tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> is calculated to be 0.42 electrons. <sentence_start/>Only 0.29 electrons were added to H2 in tI10-YH<sub>4</sub>. <sentence_start/>Finally, the formation of YH<sub>6</sub> can be described as Y + 3H<sub>2 </sub>→ YH<sub>6</sub>. <sentence_start/>In this case only, one electron is added to each H<sub>2</sub> and the H-H bond is elongated to 1.31 Å, in close agreement with the “molecular” H<sub>2</sub> in YH<sub>4</sub>. <sentence_start/>In cI14-YH<sub>6</sub>, each H atom has accepted 0.25 electrons, which is not enough to dissociate the H<sub>2</sub> molecule.

A previous study<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation> has shown that 4<italic toggle="yes">s</italic>-3<italic toggle="yes">d</italic> charge transfer turns Ca from <italic toggle="yes">s</italic>-dominant into <italic toggle="yes">s</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">d</italic> dominant at high pressure, similar to the electronic configuration of Y atom. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the presence of same structure types in YH<sub>4</sub> (YH<sub>6</sub>) and CaH<sub>4</sub> (CaH<sub>6</sub>) is not accidental. <sentence_start/>However, the H-H distance of “H<sub>2</sub>” molecule in YH<sub>4</sub> (1.33 Å) is much longer than that (0.81 Å) in CaH<sub>4</sub> at 120 GPa as Y transfer one more valence electron to H<sub>2</sub> than Ca resulting in a longer H-H distance in YH<sub>4</sub> (YH<sub>6</sub>). <sentence_start/>The empirical consideration is support from quantitative calculations of the difference of the electron density of tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> to that of a hypothetical structure consisting only H sublattice. <sentence_start/>It is clearly shown in Fig. 3(a,b), that there is no electron density (covalent bond) between the two H2 atoms in the pure H structure. <sentence_start/>However, when the Y atoms were present, localized electrons are found between two H2 atoms. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the charge transfer from Y to H2 is responsible to the formation of molecular “H<sub>2</sub>” in YH<sub>4</sub>. <sentence_start/>Similarly, the foramtion of “H<sub>6</sub>” hexagons in YH<sub>6</sub> results from the accommodation by H of excess electrons from Y atom (Fig. 3c,d). <sentence_start/>For comparison, a survey of molecular “H<sub>2</sub>” in most hydrogen-rich compounds only show a slightly elongated H-H bond length than pure solid H<sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>Examples are 0.87 Å in GeH<sub>4</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b7" pmid="18851245" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.107002" count="1">7</citation>, 0.79 Å in SnH<sub>4</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b6" doi="10.1073/pnas.0908342107" pmcid="PMC2824346" pmid="20080576" count="1">6</citation>, 0.84 Å in SiH<sub>2</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b15" doi="10.1073/pnas.1007354107" pmcid="PMC2936615" pmid="20798059" count="1">15</citation>, 0.76 Å in LiH<sub>2</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b16" doi="10.1073/pnas.0908262106" pmcid="PMC2764941" pmid="19805046" count="1">16</citation> and 0.8 Å in NaH<sub>9</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b17" pmid="21770539" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.106.237002" count="1">17</citation>.

The electronic properties, lattice dynamical and electron-phonon coupling parameter (EPC) of tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> and cI14-YH<sub>6</sub> have been calculated. <sentence_start/>Both tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> and cI14-YH<sub>6</sub> are found to be metals from the band structures presented in Fig. <sentence_start/>4. <sentence_start/>We found three features common to tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> and cI14-YH<sub>6</sub>: (i) the large densiy of states at the Fermi level (<italic toggle="yes">N</italic><sub>F</sub>), 0.44 eV<sup>−1</sup> per f.u. in tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> and 0.6 eV<sup>−1</sup> per f.u. in cI14-YH<sub>6</sub> at 120 GPa; (ii) the concurrence of falt and steep electronic bands near the <italic toggle="yes">N</italic><sub>F</sub>, providing a possibility of the pairing of eletrons at the <italic toggle="yes">N</italic><sub>F</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b30" count="1">30</citation>; (iii) strong Y-H hybridization derived from the significant overlap of Y- and H-DOS. <sentence_start/>Note that in a preivous study<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b9" pmid="19792676" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.077002" count="1">9</citation> it was demonstrated that the Y-H hybridization is responsible for the superconductivity in YH<sub>3</sub>.

Figure 5 shows the calculated phonon dispersions, phonon density of states (PHDOS), Eliashberg spectral function (<italic toggle="yes">α</italic><sup>2</sup>F(ω)/ω)and EPC integrated (λ(ω))for tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> and cI14-YH<sub>6</sub> at 120 GPa. <sentence_start/>The absence of any imaginary phonon modes proves the dynamical stabilities of both compounds. <sentence_start/>As expected, both phonon spectra are separeted into two frequency regions, with the low frequencies (<10 THz) dominated by the vibrations of Y atom while the high end of the spectra by H atoms. <sentence_start/>In tI10-YH<sub>4</sub>, the resulting EPC parameter λ is 1.01 at 120 GPa, which is comparable to the maximum value (~1.4<sup>9</sup>) predicted for fcc-YH<sub>3</sub>. <sentence_start/>Note that the low-frequency vibrations contribute to 18% of the total λ while the ramaining 82% comes from H vibrations. <sentence_start/>Circles with radius proportional to the EPC were also plotted in Fig. 6 to illustrate the contributions associated with different phonon modes. <sentence_start/>One can observe that nearly all phonon modes contribute to the overall λ, reflecting a three-dimensional nature of the structure.

Surprisingly, according to the calculation, the EPC parameter λ of cI14-YH<sub>6</sub> reaches 2.93 at 120 GPa, even larger than that (2.69 at 150 GPa<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation>) in cI14-CaH<sub>6</sub>. <sentence_start/>However, the Eliashberg phonon spectral functions of cI14-CaH<sub>6</sub> and cI14-YH<sub>6</sub> are quite different. <sentence_start/>The EPC in cI14-CaH<sub>6</sub> was derived primarily from the two phonon modes (<italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>2g</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">E</italic><sub>g</sub>) at the zone center Γ point. <sentence_start/>However, we observed an overall contribution of different modes to λ along N-P-Γ-N directions. <sentence_start/>Moreover, 90% of the total λ is contributed by H vibrations. <sentence_start/>The superconductivity in YH<sub>6</sub> is associated with the Kohn anomalies observed in the phonon dispersion of the phonon branch Γ-H and H-N. <sentence_start/>The calculation of the nesting function (Fig. 5c) confirms this expectation and clearly show strong nesting along Γ-H and H-N directions. <sentence_start/>Compare to the other 5 bands crossing the Fermi level, the Fermi surface of strongly nested band (Fig. 6c) shows a complex “vase”-like topology with strong nesting along Γ-H.

<italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> was estimated from the spectral function (<italic toggle="yes">α</italic><sup>2</sup>F(μ)) by numerically solving the Eliashberg equations<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b31" count="1">31</citation> with typical choice of Coulomb pseudopotential <italic toggle="yes">μ</italic>* = 0.1−0.13. <sentence_start/>The Coulomb repulsion is taken into account in terms of the <italic toggle="yes">μ</italic>* scaled to a cutoff frequency<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b32" count="1">32</citation>. <sentence_start/>At 120 GPa, the calculated <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> is 84-95 K for tI10-YH<sub>4</sub>, much higher than the maximal 40 K predicted for fcc-YH<sub>3</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b9" pmid="19792676" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.077002" count="1">9</citation>. <sentence_start/>Note that tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> has a much larger logarithmic average frequency of 1119 K than fcc-YH<sub>3</sub> (350 K<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b9" pmid="19792676" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.077002" count="1">9</citation>) due to the presence of molecular “H<sub>2</sub>”, which helps to enhance the superconductivity. <sentence_start/>For cI14-YH<sub>6</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> value of 251-264 K was estimated. <sentence_start/>This value is comparable to the predicted <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> (220-235 K at 150 GPa) in CaH<sub>6</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation>. <sentence_start/>Although, in principle, there is no upper limit to the <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> value within the Midgal-Eliashberg theory, remarks on the very high <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> value of cI14-YH<sub>6</sub> must be view with caution. <sentence_start/>The EPC calculations were based on the harmonic approximation and without the consideration of electron correction effects. <sentence_start/>A previous study<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b38" count="1">38</citation> had shown that anharmonicity of atomic motion may reduce or even suppress the superconductivity of AlH<sub>3</sub> due to the renormalization of the lower vibration modes by anharmonicity<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b33" pmid="23215200" doi="10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.175502" count="1">33</citation>. <sentence_start/>However, this suggestion is contrary to the observation that anharmonic vibraions will significantly enhance <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> in case of disordered compounds<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b34" count="1">34</citation>. <sentence_start/>Another important, but often neglected, situation is that the Fermi level topology may be altered in improved electronic band structure including corrections to self interaction and electron correlation effects. <sentence_start/>In AH<sub>3</sub>, the parallel bands favouring nesting disappeared in the GW calculated band structure<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b35" count="1">35</citation>. <sentence_start/>Here, <italic toggle="yes">GW</italic> band struture calculations were performed for tI10-YH<sub>4</sub> and cI14-YH<sub>6</sub>. <sentence_start/>No significant change in the band structures, particularly for the bands near or crossing the Fermi level, was found in both case (Fig. 4). <sentence_start/>Therefore, the discussion presented above will still be valid and we expect YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> are good Methods

Structure predictions for YH<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic> were performed using the particle swarm optimization technique implemented in the CALYPSO code<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b36" count="1">36</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b37" count="1">37</citation>. <sentence_start/>In recent studies, it was shown that the approach was successful on the prediction of high pressure structures on both elemental and binary compounds, such as N<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b38" count="1">38</citation>, Ca-H<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b22" doi="10.1073/pnas.1118168109" pmcid="PMC3340045" pmid="22492976" count="1">22</citation>, H<sub>2</sub>S<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b11" pmid="24811660" doi="10.1063/1.4874158" count="1">11</citation> and BeH<sub>2</sub><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b39" pmid="24697470" doi="10.1063/1.4869145" count="1">39</citation>. <sentence_start/>In this work, systematic structure search were performed on six stoichiometries (YH<sub>2</sub>, YH<sub>3</sub>, YH<sub>4</sub>, YH<sub>5</sub>, YH<sub>6</sub> and YH<sub>8</sub>) at 100 and 150 GPa. <sentence_start/>Model cells up to 4 formula units (f.u.) for each stoichiometry were used. <sentence_start/>The structure search was considered converged when~1000 successive structures were generated after a lowest energy structure was found.

<italic toggle="yes">ab initio</italic> structure relaxations were performed using density functional theory within the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation (GGA) as implemented in the Vienna <italic toggle="yes">ab initio</italic> simulation package (VASP)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b40" doi="10.1103/physrevb.54.11169" pmid="9984901" count="1">40</citation>. <sentence_start/>The band structures were calculated with both PBE-GGA and <italic toggle="yes">GW</italic> methods<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b41" count="1">41</citation>. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">GW</italic> interpolated band structures were computed using WANNIER90<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b42" count="1">42</citation>. <sentence_start/>The all-electron projector augmented wave (PAW)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b43" count="1">43</citation> method was adopted with 1<italic toggle="yes">s</italic> and 4<italic toggle="yes">s</italic><sup>2</sup>4<italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>6</sup>4<italic toggle="yes">d</italic><sup>1</sup>5<italic toggle="yes">s</italic><sup>2</sup> treated as valence electrons for H and Y, respectively. <sentence_start/>An energy cutoff of 700 eV and a Monkhorst-Pack Brillouin zone sampling grid with a resolution of 0.5 Å<sup>−1</sup> were used in the structure searches. <sentence_start/>Selected low energy structures were then re-optimized with a denser grid better than 0.2 Å<sup>−1</sup> and a higher energy cutoff of 1000 eV. <sentence_start/>Phonon dispersion and electron-phonon coupling (EPC) calculations were performed with density functional perturbation theory using the Quantum-ESPRESSO package<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="b44" count="1">44</citation>. <sentence_start/>Norm-conserving pseudopotentials for Y and H were considered with a kinetic energy cutoff of 140 Ry. 8 <sentence_start/>× 8 × 8 (59 <italic toggle="yes">q</italic>-points) and 10 × 10 × 10 (47 <italic toggle="yes">q</italic>-points) <italic toggle="yes">q</italic>-meshes in the first Brillouin zones were used in the EPC calculations for YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub>, respectively. <sentence_start/>Monkhorst-Pack grids of 32 × 32 × 32 and 40 × 40 × 40 were used to ensure <italic toggle="yes">k</italic>-points sampling convergence with Gaussians of width 0.03 Ry for YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub>, respectively, in order to approximate the zero-width limit in the calculations of the EPC parameter, λ.
Conclusion

In conclusion, structure predictions have demonstrated that yttrium atom can react with more than three hydrogens under pressure. <sentence_start/>Two high-hydride phases, YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub>, were predicted to be thermodynamically stable relative to YH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> above 110 GPa. <sentence_start/>At the stable pressure ranges, YH<sub>4</sub> has a bct strucure containing both moniatomic H and molecular “H<sub>2</sub>” while YH<sub>6</sub> adopted a bcc structure with a H sodalite-like cage. <sentence_start/>Electron-phonon coupling calculations show that both YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> are supercodncutive with <italic toggle="yes">T</italic><sub>c</sub> higher than YH<sub>3</sub>. <sentence_start/>The results presented here support the suggestion that compressing the mixture of elements (compounds) and hydrogen is a way to search high-temperature superconductors. <sentence_start/>In addition, in principle, YH<sub>4</sub> and YH<sub>6</sub> can be synthesized by compressing the mixture of YH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> above 110 GPa.
